description: GitGoblins is a team of COMSATS University Islamabad students. We are checking whether NASA satellite and reanalysis data can independently confirm the climate trends Pakistan's weather service reports for 1981 to 2025: where it is changing, by how much, and whether the change is statistically real. Our team is complete. All six members are confirmed at the Topi Local Event.
summary:
𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. Has Pakistan’s temperature changed since 1981, and do days and nights change in the same way?

𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮. Daily NASA POWER data (MERRA-2 reanalysis) for 38 places across Pakistan, 1981 to 2025. NASA GISTEMP, a second NASA analysis built from weather stations, is a cross check for average temperature.

𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗱. For each place and season we measured the change per decade (Theil Sen slope, 95% range from a block bootstrap) and tested significance with a Mann Kendall test, corrected for checking 38 places at once. A hand check of 5 places against NASA’s own data viewer matched on all 30 values.

𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀. Night time lows have warmed by 0.20 °C per decade nationally (range 0.08 to 0.32), a significant change. Summer daytime highs have fallen in 25 of 38 places by enough to pass the same test. Over the whole year, daytime highs show no clear trend.

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗻. Figures from Pakistan’s weather service (PMD), as reported in press, sit next to ours. Its night time figure is inside the NASA range and its daytime high figure is outside it.

𝗟𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘀. Night lows show a level step near 1997 to 1998, which NASA documents can come from new satellite instruments, so we also show 1998 to 2025. Each place is a 50 km grid cell, not a station.

𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻. Day and night change differently, and one average temperature hides that.
details:
What it does

Indus Detective is a free website that answers one question: is Pakistan getting hotter? A visitor picks a place (38 NASA grid cells, each about 50 km wide), a measure (average temperature, daytime high or night time low), a season and a period. The site shows the yearly values, the change per decade, a 95% range and a plain verdict: statistically significant, not conclusive or no clear trend. A dot map shows where change is strongest. The opening lines and four finding cards give the answer before any controls.

What we found

  • Night time lows have warmed by 0.20 °C per decade nationally (range 0.08 to 0.32), a significant change.
  • Spring nights have warmed by 0.39 °C per decade, and 36 of 38 places pass the test.
  • Summer daytime highs have fallen in 25 of 38 places by enough to pass the same test. The national average for summer highs is not conclusive.
  • The summer gap between day and night is shrinking, by 0.50 °C per decade.
  • Pakistan’s weather service (PMD), as reported in press, shows a night time figure inside the NASA range and a daytime high figure outside it.

How it works

We use daily NASA POWER data built from the MERRA-2 reanalysis, 1981 to 2025, and compute our own daily means. We measure each trend with a Theil Sen slope and a 95% range from a block bootstrap. We test it with a Mann Kendall test and correct for checking 38 places at once. A change counts as significant only if it passes the test and its range excludes zero. NASA GISTEMP, built from weather stations, is a cross check for average temperature. A break check looks for sudden level steps. All results are precomputed into data files, so the site is fast and has no live data calls.

Benefits and intended impact

Students, teachers, journalists and the public get a clear, checkable picture of how temperature has changed where they live. Day and night are shown separately, which a single average hides. Every hard term opens a plain English meaning. A Concise view keeps it simple, and an Extended view opens every number for people who want them. The code is open, so anyone can rerun the analysis.

What makes it creative

  • The findings are told as case files: nights versus days, spring, and summer days. Each has one claim and one chart.
  • NASA and PMD figures sit on one chart, so agreement and difference are visible at a glance.
  • Uncertainty is shown, not hidden. A non significant result is reported as a finding.

Factors we considered

  • A reanalysis is a model, not a weather station, so the site says so.
  • NASA documents that new satellite instruments can create level steps in reanalysis. Our night lows show a step near 1997 to 1998, so we show 1998 to 2025 next to the full period.
  • We hand checked 5 places against NASA’s own data viewer, and all 30 values matched.
  • Rainfall is not shown, because the source values were not reliable for trends.
  • The PMD figures come from press coverage of its 2026 report, because we could not find the report itself. The site labels them that way.
  • Teammates tested the site on phones.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, netCDF4, requests) for the analysis. React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS for the site. Hosted on Vercel. Code on GitHub under the MIT licence.

Links

Live site: https://indus-detective.vercel.app
Source code: https://github.com/thehassanbukhari/indus-detective
